title: Lesson Planning — The Deep Dive

pts: State the lesson's aim as an observable can-do: 'learners can ask for and give directions,' not 'learners will study directions.'
Choose activities only after the aim is fixed — the aim should never be reverse-engineered from a favourite activity.
A vague aim produces a vague lesson, however polished the materials look.

items: Take five lesson titles from your textbook (for example, ‘Unit 4: Food’).
For each, write the aim as a topic (Food vocabulary), then rewrite it as a can-do (Learners can order a meal and ask about ingredients).
For each can-do, write how you will see it happen in the lesson (In pairs, learners role-play ordering at a dhaba).
Check: does every activity in the textbook lesson help learners reach the can-do? Mark any that do not.
Decide what to cut, change or add.
Work with a colleague and swap aims to check whether they are observable.
Write aims with learners: ‘What do you want to be able to do by the end of this unit?’
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Topic: Past simple. → Can-do: Learners can tell a partner about their last holiday.
Topic: Reading comprehension on the water cycle. → Can-do: Learners can explain the water cycle in their own words using a diagram.
Topic: Letter writing. → Can-do: Learners can write a short letter to the headteacher requesting a sports day.

blocks.x: A quick test for any aim: Could an observer see this happening by the end of the lesson?

body: Purpose: to show the transformation of an aim. Content: a three-step vertical flow. Top box: ‘Topic: Food’. Arrow down to middle box: ‘Can-do: Learners can order a meal and ask about ingredients’. Arrow down to bottom box: ‘Evidence: pairs role-play ordering at a dhaba’. A small eye icon beside the bottom box labelled ‘observable’. Style: clean, two colours. Board version: three lines with arrows.

items: Google Docs (free). Keep a running document of aims for a term, organized by unit, so you can see how aims build on one another.

blocks.x: Write the can-do at the top of each page in your lesson diary before planning anything else.

pts: Lead-in, presentation, controlled practice, freer practice, production, wrap-up — each stage builds on the last.
Skipping controlled practice and jumping to production usually surfaces errors that a staged build-up would have prevented.
The arc is a default, not a law — some lessons (task-based ones, for instance) reorder it deliberately.

items: Start from your can-do aim.
Plan the stages: lead-in, presentation or input, controlled practice, freer practice, production, wrap-up.
For each stage, write one line: what learners do, and how it prepares for the next stage.
Check that no stage jumps too far from the previous one (for example, from presentation straight to free production).
Teach the lesson. Afterwards, mark any stage where learners struggled and note whether the stage before it was enough preparation.
For a task-based lesson, use the task cycle instead (Unit 6, Unit 28).
For a skills lesson, use pre-, while- and post- stages (Unit 3).
Support: for weaker classes, add a second controlled practice stage.
Stretch: for stronger classes, shorten controlled practice and extend production.

blocks.x: A staged plan for ‘Learners can describe their neighbourhood’ (A2):

lines: Lead-in (5): photos of three neighbourhoods; learners say which they like.
Input (10): teacher describes her own neighbourhood; learners note places.
Language focus (8): There is / there are, prepositions of place.
Controlled practice (8): learners complete sentences about a map.
Freer practice (12): pairs draw and describe their own neighbourhood.
Wrap-up (2): exit ticket.

body: Purpose: to show how stages build. Content: a gently rising curve from left to right, like a hill. Along the curve, six labelled points: lead-in, input, language focus, controlled practice, freer practice, wrap-up. The height of the curve represents ‘learner independence’, rising steadily. Style: smooth curve, labelled points. Board version: a rising line with six dots.

items: Google Sheets (free). A staging grid template with columns for stage, time, aim of stage, interaction and materials.

blocks.x: A paper staging grid (Appendix), filled in by hand.

points.sub: Plan the difficulty, not just the content
pts: Predict where learners will struggle with form, meaning, or pronunciation before the lesson, not during it.
Prepared solutions — a clearer example, a CCQ, a quick timeline — turn a stumble into a smooth moment.
This single habit prevents most of the visible 'winging it' moments in an otherwise solid lesson.

v: The ‘anticipated problems’ box in the plan template

items: Before teaching new language, ask three questions: what might learners find hard about its meaning, its form, and its pronunciation?
For each problem, write a solution: an example, a CCQ, a timeline, a drill.
Also predict one problem with the task itself (instructions, timing, grouping).
Teach. Tick problems that did arise; note any you did not predict.
Keep a list of ‘problems I did not predict’. It becomes a valuable personal reference.
Plan with a colleague who knows the class.
Ask a learner from the previous year which parts of the unit were hardest.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Meaning: learners may think it means ‘usually’ in the present. → CCQ: Does she still do it?
Form: confusion with be used to. → Keep them apart; teach be used to later.
Pronunciation: /ˈjuːst tə/ often said /ˈjuːstə/; learners may say /ˈjuːzd tuː/. → Model and drill the reduced form.
Task: pairs may finish quickly. → Prepare an extension question.

body: Purpose: to structure the prediction. Content: a target language item in the centre (used to). Three magnifying glasses around it labelled ‘Meaning’, ‘Form’, ‘Pronunciation’, each with a short example problem and a small ‘solution’ tag attached. Style: clean, radial layout. Board version: not applicable.

items: English Grammar Profile (Cambridge, free online). Shows at which CEFR level learners typically begin to use a structure accurately, which helps predict difficulty.

blocks.x: A notebook page per unit: ‘Problems I expected / problems that happened’.

body: Many experienced teachers say that the section of a lesson plan they value most is not the procedure but the anticipated-problems box. Thinking through what could go wrong in advance is what makes calm, quick responses possible during the lesson.

pts: Build flexible timing bands rather than exact minute counts that rarely survive contact with a real class.
Prepare one ready extension activity for early finishers and one cut option if time runs short.
A plan without contingency options forces improvisation exactly when the teacher has the least attention to spare.

items: Give each stage a time range rather than a single number (8–12 minutes).
Mark one stage that can be cut or shortened if time runs out.
Prepare one extension activity that can be added if time remains.
Mark the ‘must-do’ stage: the one that achieves the aim. Protect it.
After the lesson, note how long each stage actually took.
Keep a bank of five-minute ‘fillers’ that practise recent language (a quick quiz, a chunk race).
For forty-minute periods, plan for thirty-five and keep five in reserve.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Must-do: freer practice (pairs describe neighbourhoods).
Cut if short: controlled practice reduced to 3 sentences.
Extend if time: pairs write a short description for the class wall.
Five-minute filler: ‘I spy’ with prepositions around the classroom.

body: Purpose: to show flexible timing. Content: a horizontal bar representing a 40-minute period, divided into coloured stage blocks. Each block has a lighter extension at its end showing the possible range. One block is outlined with a thick border and labelled ‘must-do’. One block has scissors beside it (‘can cut’). At the end, a small dashed block labelled ‘extension if time’. Style: clean, colour-coded. Board version: not applicable.

items: Online Stopwatch or a phone timer to record how long stages actually take.

blocks.x: Write the planned end time of each stage in the margin of the plan and glance at the clock.

pts: Note whether each stage is teacher-led, pair, group, or individual directly on the plan.
Deliberate variety in interaction pattern sustains attention better than any single format held too long.
This connects directly to Unit 7's grouping dynamics — the plan is where that decision gets made in advance.

items: In the interaction column, mark each stage: T–Ss, S–S (pairs), GW (group work), IW (individual work).
Check the whole lesson: are there long stretches of the same pattern?
Aim for at least two changes of pattern in a forty-minute lesson.
Note who will work with whom (Unit 7).
After the lesson, note which pattern produced most learner talk.
Use icons instead of abbreviations.
For a large class, add ‘mingle’ or ‘bench groups’ as patterns.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Lead-in: T–Ss / Input: T–Ss / Language focus: IW then S–S check / Controlled practice: S–S / Freer practice: GW / Wrap-up: IW (exit ticket)

body: Purpose: a set of symbols for lesson plans. Content: five simple icons with labels: one figure facing many (‘T–Ss’), two figures facing each other (‘S–S’), four figures in a circle (‘GW’), a single figure writing (‘IW’), several figures moving (‘mingle’). Style: consistent line icons, printable small. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). Add an interaction column to the staging grid, with conditional formatting to colour each pattern.

blocks.x: Coloured pencils: one colour per interaction pattern in the margin of the paper plan.

pts: Authentic materials often need grading — simplifying vocabulary, chunking a long text — to suit the level.
Over-grading can strip out exactly the communicative richness that made the material worth using.
Grade the task around the text before grading the text itself, where possible.

v: A short authentic text (a news report, a notice, a menu)

items: Choose an authentic text slightly above the class’s level.
Instead of simplifying the text, design an easier task: find five numbers; match headings to paragraphs; true/false on the main idea.
Teach the lesson with the original text and the graded task.
For a stronger group, use a harder task on the same text (summarize; identify the writer’s opinion).
Compare learners’ reactions to authentic and simplified texts.
Where a text is truly too hard, shorten it rather than rewriting it.
Add a glossary of five key words beside the text.
Support: easier task on the same text (for example, scanning for dates).
Stretch: harder task on the same text (for example, comparing two viewpoints).

blocks.x: One text, three tasks (a newspaper report about a new metro line):

lines: Easy: Find the date the line opens and the number of stations.
Medium: Match each paragraph to a heading.
Harder: What are two arguments for and one against the new line?

blocks.x: When to adapt the text itself: remove sections, add a glossary, or replace a few very low-frequency words, keeping the original voice as far as possible.

body: Purpose: to show differentiation by task. Content: a single newspaper-style text in the centre. Three arrows lead out to three task cards of increasing size and colour intensity: ‘scan for facts’, ‘match headings’, ‘evaluate arguments’. Style: clean, stepped visual. Board version: not applicable.

items: Rewordify or similar simplification tools exist, but use them cautiously: they often remove the features that make a text worth reading. A glossary is usually a better support. [VERIFY current availability before recommending a named tool.]

blocks.x: Photocopy the original text; write task cards by hand at three levels.

points.sub: Plan the board like a slide
pts: Sketch the board plan in advance — what goes where, and in what order it appears.
A cluttered, unplanned board undermines even a well-staged lesson by confusing the visual record learners rely on.
Reserve a consistent board zone for target language so learners know where to look for it.

v: A sketch of the board on paper

items: Divide your board sketch into zones: date and aim (top), target language (a fixed box), working space (centre), vocabulary (side).
Decide what will go where, and in what order it will appear.
Decide what stays up for the whole lesson (aim, target language) and what will be erased.
Teach. At the end of the lesson, photograph the board (or sketch it).
Compare the actual board with your plan. Was the key language easy to find?
Use consistent colours: one for new language, one for examples, one for corrections.
Ask a learner to copy the board plan for the class record.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A board plan for the neighbourhood lesson:

lines: Top left: date, can-do aim.
Right column: new vocabulary (post office, pharmacy, bus stop, opposite, next to).
Centre: map of a neighbourhood, used for examples.
Bottom box: target structures (There is a pharmacy next to the bank.)
Bottom right corner: ‘Good language / Fix it’ for feedback (Unit 1).

body: Purpose: a model board layout. Content: a rectangle representing a blackboard, divided into labelled zones: ‘Aim’ (top left), ‘New words’ (right column), ‘Working space’ (centre, with a simple map), ‘Key language’ (a boxed area bottom centre), ‘Feedback’ (bottom right). Style: chalk-like but clean; each zone lightly tinted. Board version: as described.

items: Phone camera. Photograph the board at the end of each lesson and share it with absent learners or keep it as a record.

blocks.x: A notebook sketch of the board before the lesson, as in the activity.

body: Keep the aim and the key language in the same place on the board every lesson. Learners soon learn where to look, and absent-minded copying becomes purposeful note-taking.

pts: After each lesson, note briefly what worked, what didn't, and why — before the details fade.
Reflection closes the loop between planning and classroom craft, turning one lesson's outcome into the next lesson's input.
Over a course, this habit compounds into planning that improves cyclically rather than repeating the same gaps.
points.who: Donald Schön, "The Reflective Practitioner"; Richards & Lockhart

v: A reflection page in the lesson diary

items: Immediately after the lesson, answer three questions in writing: What worked? What did not? What will I change next time?
Add one piece of evidence for each answer (an exit-ticket result, an observation, a learner comment).
Before planning the next lesson, reread your reflection.
Once a month, read all your reflections for a class and look for patterns.
Share one reflection with a colleague and ask for their view.
Record a voice note on your phone instead of writing.
Use a ‘lesson in three words’ summary for busy days.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Worked: pairs drawing their neighbourhoods; lots of talk. Evidence: 28 of 32 exit tickets correct.
Didn’t work: my instructions for the controlled practice; three pairs started the wrong exercise.
Change: demonstrate first next time, then ICQs.

blocks.x: Reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action (Schön 1983): the first happens during the lesson (you notice confusion and give an extra example); the second happens afterwards (you ask why the confusion happened and change the plan).

body: Purpose: to show planning and reflection as one cycle. Content: a circle with four segments: ‘Plan’ (notebook icon), ‘Teach’ (board icon), ‘Reflect’ (thought bubble icon), ‘Revise’ (pencil icon). Small inner arrows show ‘reflection-in-action’ looping within ‘Teach’. Style: clean cycle diagram. Board version: four words in a circle.

items: Google Keep or any notes app (free). A reflection note for each lesson, labelled by class.

blocks.x: The last page of each lesson plan, kept for three questions.

body: For two weeks, write the three reflection questions after every lesson with one class only. At the end, read them all at once. Most teachers find one recurring pattern they had not noticed day to day.

dek: Unit 9 of 100: from a single measurable aim to a staged arc, anticipated problems, flexible timing, and the reflective habit that improves every plan after it.

aims.x: This unit treats the lesson plan as a thinking tool rather than a form to fill in. It works through the decisions a plan should record, from the aim to the board layout, and ends with the reflection that turns each lesson into better planning for the next.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: write lesson aims as observable, can-do outcomes;
stage a lesson so that each stage prepares for the next;
anticipate problems with meaning, form and pronunciation and plan solutions;
build flexible timing and contingency options into a plan;
plan interaction patterns deliberately;
adapt materials by grading the task before the text;
plan the board as carefully as the activities;
reflect after a lesson in a way that improves the next one.

why: Why this matters. A plan is not a script to survive — it is a tool for making deliberate decisions in advance, so that in-the-moment judgement (Unit 7) has something solid to work from.

background.x: Most teachers learn to plan lessons twice. The first time is in training, where plans are long, detailed documents written for a tutor. The second time is on the job, where plans shrink to a few lines in a diary, or disappear into the teacher’s head. Both have their uses, but both can miss the point. A lesson plan is valuable not because it is written down but because writing it forces decisions to be made before the class begins, when there is time to think, rather than during it, when there is not.

Good planning starts at the end. Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe (2005) called this backward design: decide what learners should be able to do by the end, decide how you will know they can, and only then choose activities. The idea has a long history in education and applies naturally to language teaching, where the aim is usually a communicative ability (learners can ask for and give directions) rather than a piece of content (directions vocabulary).

A plan is also a record for reflection. Donald Schön (1983) distinguished between reflection-in-action, the quick adjustments a practitioner makes while working, and reflection-on-action, the slower thinking afterwards. The plan supports both: it gives the teacher a reference point during the lesson and a basis for asking, afterwards, what happened and why.

In Indian schools, planning often has to fit within prescribed textbooks, fixed periods of thirty-five or forty minutes, and institutional formats for lesson notes. The principles in this unit work within those constraints. A textbook lesson still benefits from a clear aim, a sensible sequence and a moment of reflection, however the plan is recorded.

items: Aim achievement. For each lesson, record the proportion of learners who showed the can-do (from exit tickets or observation). Track over a month.
Timing accuracy. Compare planned and actual stage timings for a week. Adjust your estimates.
Problem prediction. Count how many of the problems that arose you had predicted. The proportion should rise as you get to know a class.
Reflection use. Check that each new plan responds to at least one point from the previous reflection.
How do you usually write lesson aims? Could an observer see them being achieved?
Which stage of your lessons is most often cut short? What does that tell you about your planning?
How do you use your textbook’s lesson plans? Which parts do you follow, adapt or skip?
What does your board look like at the end of a lesson? What would a learner copying it understand?
When do you reflect on your teaching, and what do you do with the reflections?

terms.def: The difficulties with meaning, form, pronunciation or the task that a teacher predicts learners may have, recorded in a lesson plan together with possible solutions.
Planning that begins with the intended outcomes, then decides how they will be assessed, and only then chooses activities (Wiggins and McTighe 2005); also called backward planning.
A planned layout of what will be written on the board during a lesson, such as key vocabulary, target structures and the lesson aim, so that the board supports learning clearly.
A lesson aim written as what learners will be able to do by the end, such as ‘I can ask for and give directions to a place in my town.’
A backup plan or activity prepared in case part of a lesson takes more or less time than expected or does not work as planned.
Practice in which learners use new language in a limited and supported way, such as drills or gap-fills, with a focus on accuracy.
A lesson stage in which learners use the target language with less teacher control and more choice, for example in a discussion or role-play, following controlled practice.

Adjusting the difficulty of what learners must do with a text rather than simplifying the text itself. With an authentic notice, for example, weaker learners find three facts while stronger learners interpret its tone.
The way learners are organized to interact in a stage of a lesson, such as teacher–class, pairs, groups or individual work.

The short opening stage of a lesson that engages learners’ interest, activates what they already know about the topic and prepares them for the main input; for example, showing a photo of a local market before a shopping dialogue.
A clear statement of what learners should be able to do by the end of a lesson, ideally written as a can-do statement, for example ‘Learners can ask for and give directions to places in their town’.
One distinct phase of a lesson with its own purpose, such as lead-in, presentation, controlled practice, freer practice or wrap-up; each stage should prepare learners for the next.

Changing published or existing materials to suit a particular class, by omitting, adding, simplifying, reordering or personalizing content; for example, replacing a foreign setting in a textbook dialogue with a local one.

Thinking about and adjusting one’s practice while it is happening, such as changing an activity mid-lesson when learners are confused (Schön 1983). It contrasts with reflection-on-action, which takes place after the event.

Looking back on practice after the event in order to understand it and plan improvements, for example writing notes after a lesson or discussing it with a colleague (Schön 1983). It complements reflection-in-action.
